On section 8-compulsory purchase:

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
I wish to offer a slight amendment to clause 8, or rather I suggest it to the minister in the hope that it will he acceptable. But before doing so, I would like to make a few general observations regarding the way in which this proposition actually works out from the standpoint of the soldier as an applicant. It was my privilege to spend some two months on the mainland in British Columbia endeavouring to do what I could for the returned man in his effort to find a home upon the land, and having had some experience in the city of Vancouver during the last few months, I have no hesitation whatever in most heartily congratulating the Government and the minister upon the comprehensive, complete, and in the main, thoroughly satisfactory character of the scheme which has been placed before the country. I want also to congratulate the minister upon the staff which is to be found in the city of Vancouver, and I presume a similar staff in the matter of efficiency has been provided in every other office throughout the country. I mention the Vancouver staff because I know of it, and know something of its character and efficiency. Not only do I refer to the officials, 'but also to the men who comprise the qualification committee and the advisory board.' In the city of Vancouver there are three of the best known loan men in the province of British Columbia, who volunteered their services. I do not suppose we could have bought those services; the men are too busy, their time is too valuable, and they are otherwise engaged from morning to night; but as a contribution by themselves towards this work they were willing to help and do it gratuitously. This service was very highly appreciated by the board in Vancouver, and I am sure is likewise appreciated by this House, and I presume similar conditions obtain with regard to other centres.
The question may arise in some men's minds: Who are going back to the land? We of course looked for men who had come from the farm to return, but in addition we found that there was a considerable number of men from offices, even some men from the professions, who desired to settle upon the land and for various reasons, now consider, they do not further desire the confinement of an office. They seek and long for, a settled life; they want to be doing what they believe is worth while. They appreciate the national slogan of production as the cry for the coming generation, and wish to make their contribution towards the development of this great country. We did find, however, that there are in the province, and I presume the same may obtain in otheT provinces, several misconceptions as to the character and the nature of the scheme outlined. We found in some parts of British Columbia men here and there with the idea that, the Government was buying on a large scale, that it was purchasing great areas of land. Consequently, we had offers from individuals and corporations of land that was in their opinion, most admirably suited for the returned soldiers. Some men seemed to think they had land that was especially suitable for the returned men, although to the most of us the question would naturally occur why it had not been offered and accepted for a similar purpose prior to the introduction of this scheme.
Notw I want to speak of a matter which the minister did not mention but which is one of the practical outcroppings of the entire proposition. We have received very hearty co-operation from various organized bodies, from municipalities, and from private citizens, and indeed from 5 p.m. real estate firms, along these lines. A man returned wished to engage in a certain kind of farming. We knew the country and would say to him: "Go out to a certain place. Go to Mr. Smith and he will show you everything in that district which is available." There was nothing in it for Mr. Smith, he did that work in the interests of the men con-

cerned; and thus we were able to facilitate the search of the applicant for land without any material expense.
I made reference to real estate agents. Mr. Chairman, I want to say that in this country, and I do not speak from the standpoint of any one province, there are real estate men, and real estate men, and there is a vast difference between them. In the latter class the manhood still dominates, the adjective is smaller than ithe man. We did receive very material assistance from a great number of real estate offices and many of the men in those offices have given their time and their services in order to secure settlers upon the land. I regret to say, however, that in a few cases it was necessary to discontinue operations with certain men who seemed to possess the spirit of the age to such an extent that they deemed it was up to them to got all they could, not simply out of the Government- but they seemed to think it was their chance to "do" the soldier and it was our business according to the best information we could secure, and ito the extent of our ability to safeguard the interest of the returned man who was seeking a home upon the land.
The question has been raided as to the character of the land upon which these men went. I do not want any one to think that in every case the returned men are settling upon entirely new land. That is not the case, Sir. In some instances they are buying unimproved land, but more generally in the province of British Columbia they are purchasing improved land. It may be argued that this does not really conduce to an increased amount of production, but the reason for that, Sir, is this: In many sections of that province you will find a large number of farms and ranches held by elderly men. The explanation of that is that his boys have gone overseas and will not return.
He has a farm on his hands, he is too old to work, and he says: " I will sell it." In many cases he offers his farm for sale at a cheap price to the returned man, and he himself steps aside and gives him the advantage of his years of toil. That is one reason, Sir, why in many cases they have bought improved property. I could cite instance after instance where that has actually taken place; the elderly father who is left on the farm is not able to carry on, and consequently his land is sold. Often it is subdivided into two, three, four, or more small holdings, and that means the neuclei of so many more families. As a result we have a

large percentage of returned men upon the improved lands of British Columbia. I am speaking now of the southern part of the province, where the majority of the settlers are locating. There are some who choose the pioneering life, but unless a man makes that choice we do not encourage or even go so far as to suggest it to him. Most of the men want their homes' reasonably near centres, with all the advantages of social and business life that can be obtained in the older sections of the country. The result is that we are seeking more land in the southern part of the province.	[DOT]
Clause 8, as I understand it, looks towards compulsory purchase, and my amendment is along this line, Sir, that I would have the clause go a step further. I would therefore submit for the consideration of the minister and the committee the following amendment to clause 8, which would then read as follows:
The Board may, for the execution of any of the purposes of this Act, acquire by way of compulsory purchase, in the manner provided by Part III of this Act, such agricultural land as it may deem necessary from :
(a) All persons, firms, and corporations in
any part of Canada ;
(lb) The Indian superintendent for the
province of British Columbia.
I note in the Indian Act of 1906 a provision foT the appointment of an Indian superintendent for the province of British Columbia. If that appointment has not been made, a change in the wording of my amendment I presume would toe necessary. But I wish to call the attention of the Committee to two or three very important facts. In the province of British Columbia we have a large area of land held as Indian reserve land. A year ago I called the attention of the House to this matter, and again last spring. My attention has been directed to the same matter very frequently during the past two months, and I would not be performing what I believe to be my duty and taking the right course unless I gave some additional facts regarding this very acute situation in that province.
I presume that these Indian reserves were granted years ago on' the principle that the Indian was the ward of the Government, that he was to be taken care of by the Government, that he was not in a position to look after himself; and that therefore a wide sweep of land should be given to him on which he could hunt and fish. In the course of time the Indian population has decreased, the hunting in the sections of the country to which I refer is altogether a thing of the past, and the result is that

in many parts of southern British Columbia we have large areas of some of the finest land utterly waste. I could cite many cases to support this statement. I have in mind a block of 800 acres of the finest land in one section of the province, occupied, I understand, by three small Indian families, who miake their living mainly by selling wood. At this juncture of the nation's history it is almost a national calamity so much of the best land in our province should thus lie waste. We pride ourselves on doing justice to the Indian. I am the last man in this House to suggest that anything but the fullest measure of justice should be meted out to him. But in doing justice to the Indian, let us not do an injustice to the white man or to the country. I have in mind another case where, adjacent to a city in British Columbia, there are some thousands of acres of choice land bordering right on the city limits, impeding most seriously the development of that city and the adjacent country. 1 might enumerate many other cases. Suffice it to say that in the southern part of the province it is a most serious problem,-in fact, in soipe places it is an almost intolerable situation, and the citizens virtually demand that the Indian be placed, in this regard, upon the same footing as the white man. In other words, that he have a good chance, and, if anything, a little better chance than the white man, but that he be not allowed to hold thousands of acres of the finest land without any pretense whatever of its being used for purposes of production.
Now, Sir, my object in introducing this amendment is simply that the same provision which applies to the purchase of speculators' land be made applicable to certain Indian Reserves, and that where it can be shown that there is thus a large area of land unused, and that in all human probability it will remain unused, that the department he required to sell that land. I do not think as a matter of fact that the provisions of the amendment I suggest may ever have to be used, but if the clause is there, and it is known that we can use it, it will facilitate the purchase of such property. For this and other reasons, which I might enumerate but do not wish to take up the time of the House at the present juncture, I respectfully urge upon the minister his considering the adoption of my amendment for the benefit of returned soldiers settling in the province of British Columbia. It simply means that whatever land may be deemed necessary by the board may be
purchased not only from all persons, firms, and corporations in any part of Canada, but -with special reference to British Columbia -from the Indian superintendent for the province or other officer who has the power of acting as vendor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
Before the minister
answers that question, the Indian Land Act itself provides for the methods of procedure by which we deal with Indian lands, and I think it would be rather dangerous to adopt another method in this Act.
Mr. MEI6HEN:	From the statutory
standpoint I agree with the leader of the Opposition, that if such action were taken, it should be taken by an amendment of the Indian Act.
We have already prepared amendments to the Indian Act which will make applicable all the necessary provisions of this Act applying to returned soldiers who are Indians arid which will make the Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs take the place of the Soldier's Settlement Board in the administration of that phase of the Act,
The point raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey) is one of the most important that the committee has to consider; it was referred to some weeks ago by the member for Selkirk (Mr. Hay). When the Bill was under consideration providing for the expropriation of small portions of land on Indian reserves for public purposes, it was urged that we should not deal with Indian Reserve lands on the same principles as those upon which we dealt with private lands. It is a matter for very serious consideration indeed, whether, in view of our negotiations and settlements with the Indians in this country, which proceeded in the main, on the assumption that they were a separate nation, and that the agreements were entered into by Canada on the one hand and by the various tribes and separate peoples on the other, we ought to invade the sanctity of the treaties made and settlements arranged, for the purpose of taking their lands in order that they might be used not by the State, but by private persons. I cannot say that I have made up my mind that that argument is irresistible; I really am not disposed to think it is. It. is very questionable, though, what might result if we did take the stand urged by the member for Fraser Valley. Undoubtedly it would result in dissension, and perhaps in the issue being carried beyond the bounds of this country for settlement. No doubt, whatever settlement Canada should arrive at would,

in the end, be accepted as final; I do not suggest that any disposition to interfere would originate from without. But we have regarded these people as our wards, and we have made treaties and settlements with them; therefore it is desirable, if possible, to avoid anything in . the nature of dissension, or anything in the nature of a charge against us of infidelity. Consequently, for the present session, I have decided not to ask Parliament for power to expropriate lands in Indian Reserves for this purpose. We are now engaged in an endeavour to secure valid surrenders of these unused lands in reserves. We have officers engaged in an examination and appraisal of lands in Indian reserves in order that such are not being used and should be used for farming may be surrendered to the Crown to be used for soldier settlement. We have attained considerable success so far; with one or two exceptions, the various tribes have not been unreasonable, and if we continue this policy we are likely to succeed better than we would if we now took statutory power to expropriate. I rather think that the attitude of the various tribes will be more favourable if we proceed along the path that we have now ventured upon and try to get surrenders in every case. If the Indians should become recalcitrant, or if there should be anything in the nature of mere obstinacy as against their own interests and the interests of the State, we might consider at a later session the advis^ ability of taking expropriatory power, to be applicable in such cases For the present, I commend to the Committee the advisablity of leaving out anything in the way of power to expropriate Indian lands, and of allowing the board to deal with tho subject by employing the more conciliatory method of procuring surrender of the reserves.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
I have no thought whatever of suggesting anything which would apply to Canada as a whole. I note that provision is made in the Indian Act for action in the various provinces with regard to specific phases of legislation. I do want to impress upon the Committee and upon the minister that if there is one thing in the mind of the average citizen or returned soldier of British Columbia that is ,the cause of great unrest and discontent, it is the patent fact that much of the choicest land in the entire province is absolutely unavailable for use, and in all human probability never will be productive unless there is some radical change in the policy. Personally I do not feel disposed to give very much at-
tention to the argument that because we have always done something, we must always continue to do it. We have recognized the right of these people in the past; we have given them their opportunity. If their population is decreasing and the hunting is gone, why can we not go to these people and say: Let us make other arrangements; we will buy this land from you and give you a suitable place in which to live. We need not talk to the Indian about compulsory purchase, but steps should be taken to secure this land. We have the report of a commission regarding certain reserves which says that a certain amount of tin's land may revert to the Crown. But that amount is a very small percentage of the whole. I repeat that in British Columbia the Indian reserve question is a vital issue and is one of our grave troubles; and I ask the minister and the Government to make, at the earliest possible day, such provision as is necessary for the securing of a portion of these areas for settlement and production in order that that part of the country may develop more rapidly than it has developed in the past.
Mr. CAHiILL: Do I understand the hon. member to say that we should take this land by compulsion from the Indian?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: I ask that the provisions which apply to land held by speculators apply also to Indian reserve lands. Here is a man who has 500 acres; he is holding it until some of us will go round him and improve the value of the land so that he may grow rich out of our efforts and our labour. That man should be compelled either to work his land or sell it, hence clause (a) of the section. Then, here is an Indian reserve of 500 acres with only a few Indians on it, perhaps none at all, but some band has a legal claim upon it. My point is that similar steps should be taken with respect to this land. The band should have the benefit of any financial advantage resulting from the sale of the land; the proceeds might be invested for them and they w-ould then be in the receipt of an annual income that would be of much greater benefit to them than the mere possession of those lands which they held uncultivated.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
The steps the hon. gentleman proposes we should take before going to the length of expropriation are now being taken in British Columbia, though not as widely as we purpose taking them very shortly. We are going to make most energetic efforts to reduce to the minimum uncultivated Dominion lands there, and if

we fail after exhausting all our efforts I shall be very glad if the hon. member will bring the matter up for the consideration of Parliament next session. I may do so myself.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
With that explanation I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
Amendment withdrawn.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: I trust the Dominion Government will consider very seriously before breaking their treaty engagements with the Indians. Simply because we have the power to do so, by reason of being in greater numbers, is no reason why we should break a treaty. The Indians have rights that should be respected in this country. If we respect anything we should respect our word to the Indian or to anybody else. The fact that the lands of the Indians happen to have enhanced in value by reason of white settlement is no reason why the Indians should he compelled to give up their land. There is no justification for the hon. member or the Government deciding what is best for the Indians. The Indian may very likely not be interested in the money he may get out of the land, and if he wants to keep his land I do not think this or any other Government should take it away from him. There is plenty of land in Canada for the white man for many centuries to come without taking away from the Indian forcibly land he holds more dear perhaps than my hon. friend holds the dollars we would get out of it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: The hon. member neither understands the situation in British Columbia, nor my remarks.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On sectiop 11-school lands:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
This is a very important clause which I should have referred to in my opening remarks, We cannot, of course, take school lands and sell them. We have to sell school lands in accordance with the Dominion, Lands Act by auction sale. The returned soldiers are very much interested in these school lands. Of course, they have a chance to buy at these auction sales. We do not feel that we should interfere with our administration of that trust, except with the consent of the provinces, and therefore we devised this means of arriving at the valuation by joint boards, each board to be composed of one representative of the Dominion and one representative of the province concerned. If these two report in
favour of a certain valuation, the Soldier Settlement Board will have the option of taking the land at that valuation for returned soldier purposes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.	[DOT]*
On section 15-free soldier grants:

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: I understand it will not be possible under this clause for a soldier who already owns a homestead to take up land under this scheme. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Oh, no. Owning a homestead does not prevent it at all, but if the soldier owns a homestead he can also get a soldier grant; that would make 320 acres of free land in all. On the other hand, if the soldier has the soldier grant he is still entitled to a homestead. We say that in the case of a man who is entitled to a soldier entry and exercises his right, we cannot also undertake to assist him by way of purchasing land. We decided that the better distribution would be to deal with him as a soldier entrant, and we advance him the money accordingly, but we do not deal with him in the capacity of a buyer of private land from the board. Of course, the board has power in a special case to allow him to buy a small amount of land.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-conditions of sale and conveyance of lands by board to settlers :

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Would the minister explain paragraph (b) ? Does that mean there has to be an exact price for the land ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: This is taken word for word, I think, from the Order in Council of February 11, and the reason for it is this : If we buy a quarter-section we know what we are paying for it, and we can easily decide what to sell it at, but suppose we purchase five hundred acres in a block owned by one man; three or four soldiers want that land. Then paragraph (b) applies, its purpose being to direct the board to sell each and every parcel of the five hundred acres, or five thousand, as the case may be, at its proportionate price of the whole purchase price, not based on acreage, but based on value. That is the way it is expressed, and I think correctly expressed. I understand that it is not the intention of the board to buy any parcels of land of that kind unless it has already been selected by the soldier.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
That is quite right.

Mr. IMcRENZIE: Suppose that alongside a piece of land owned by the Government there are some thousands of acres owned by a land company, and a soldier selects 100 acres or 200 acres of that company land and tells the board that he can buy it at such a price. Suppose this price is very much higher than the average price at which the Government could buy all that company land. IVould it not he better for the Government to try and acquire all that land at a lower price than, to permit it to he taken over in small parcels?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
Yes, and that is just
ithe purpose of this section. As a matter of practice we do not purchase blocks of this kind unless we have the soldiers in sight ready to purchase the land from us. In a word, we are not taking chances; we are limiting the chances altogether, I think.
Mr. iMcKENZIE: The Government should take steps to see that a higher price is not paid by taking land over in small parcels.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Oh, yes. Very frequently we save considerable money by purchasing it in block. Ten per cent is the minimum required. The maximum allowed against the land is $4,500. That is subject to very special exceptions in the case of married men of more than ordinary qualifications, who have had successful farming experience in Canada.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: The Board is to exercise its discretion in collecting the annual payments. There are to be twenty-five annual payments, or there may be fewer in the event of default. What is the provision in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: The Board has full discretion as to what it shall do in event of default. As it deems fit, it can either overlook default or cancel upon default. Everything will depend on the circumstances of the case. As a rule, of course, default will be discouraged because we do not want soldiers to get the idea that the obligation is not to be discharged.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Would it not be better not to demand payment on principal for the first year- or two while the settler, particularly in wild land, is breaking up and improving his land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
Every effort will of course be made to overcome difficulties. But where the land is such that payment cannot be made the Board will have power to grant an extension of time. In the

generality of cases, however, we expect them to commence payments at once, the only exception being in regard to the loan for stock and implements, in which case we wait two years.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: They do not pay interest the first two years?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Not on stock and implements. They do on the land.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: I would ask the permission of the Committee to return to section 14, in connection with which I should like to ask the minister a question on two points.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Very well.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
I notice a clause in reference to placing settlers with farmers for instruction in farming, and another providing for the payment of subsistence allowances to settlers, for themselves and their dependents, while such settlers are in receipt of instructional training. The minister dealt with this matter in a general way this morning. Has the Board received specific instructions as to the disbursements that will be made in these cases, and the considerations that will be allowed the farmers? What allowances will be made for the subsistence of settlers and their families?
Mr. iMEIGHEN: Provision was made in this respect early in April. The amount allowed when a man is taking instruction in the three months' course provided in all colleges is $10 per month if he is without dependents. If he has a wife it is $35, and for each child $6, with a maximum of $25 for children. If he is a widower with a child or children, $10 for each child.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: That is in addition to the free instruction and board?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Yes. If he is a married man employed with a farmer he gets $20 and $6 for each child, with a maximum of $25.	__

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
Has the minister considered the advisability of charging a rate of interest to settlers, other than members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, or those who served in the Imperial and Allied Armies, who were ordinarily resident in Canada, which would be commensurate with the expenditures involved? I think it is evident that, in order to meet the demands of Canadian isoldiers, between two and three hundred million dollars would be required.

and "while _ we will not be disposed to be critical if we lose money on account of our own soldiers, I think we should take such steps as are necessary to insure that, in the case of settlers out. of the Imperial Army or the armies of our Allies, that we shall have a fair chance of getting back the money advanced. We should also take some further precaution, by way of demanding a greater deposit on the purchase price, such an increased deposit as shall be equal to the lack of experience Which will be found among this class of settler. The soldiers of this country will always feel that they are, to a degree, responsible for the money which is advanced to them, and I do not think it would be fair to our Canadian soldiers to include in this scheme a sort of immigration policy for European people in the carrying out of which, considerable money might be lost.
Mr. MAHAR.G: Did I understand the minister to say that the payment on land will commence the first year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Is not that a mistake? It will be rather hard for men, especially when they take up new land, to make payments the first year. In fact, it will be almost impossible.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: The money is payable the first year and the amount is small because it is spread over twenty-five years more or less. No doubt there will be cases in which men starting on new prairie land will not be able, although making a living from the first, to make payments the first year or two. Ample power is provided in these cases to carry men on. But we do not want to encourage that and we should not make it a general rule that nothing should be repayable the first year or two, because many men are buying cultivated land and there is no reason why they should not pay the first year. We therefore make the agreement the .same in each case and leave its application to the particular circumstances of the individual applicant who seeks an extension.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: It would be wise, I think, to differentiate between men purchasing improved lands and those who are buying lands in the raw state. I know from personal experience that nothing takes the "ginger" out of a fello-w-if I may put it that w-ay-so much as being pressed for inidial payments overdue, and an exception might easily be made in the case of a man on soldier grant land. It would not be a difficult matter to give him an additional year the same as in regard to his stock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
I have no doubt that in the practical working out of the scheme most of the men on soldier grant land will have to be carried for the first year, and we have ample powers to do so. These loans on soldier grant land were made before I took charge of the department. The Bill wias passed previous to that, and the law laid down. That being the case I did not feel free to alter it in that regard, particularly as the board had full power to extend 'the time. I therefore decided to leave that as it .is to the operation of the board. In answer to the hon. member for Calgary, we have considered the matter of taking extra precautions with regard to overseas men. Parliament established the principle of equality in the Act of 1917, and I felt that if we were going to admit British soldiers to the benefits of the Act we should not impose extra burdens upon them. It may be that we should exercise greater precaution in their selection and take necessary precautions against loss, and for that reason this Bill is drawn to enable us to demand a higher rate down, up to 25 per cent. I purpose to insist upon that in the case of members of the'Brit-ish Army.
I do not think there should be any complaint because that will have the result of sifting out the more doubtful cases. If 25 per cent is paid down and other precautions are exercised it will be a practical assurance against any loss further than what loss there may be in the higher rate on money that is prevalent over and above what it will be later on; but as time goes on there is every reason to believe that that difference will be eliminated. It cannot be possible that on Dominion debentures the interest will be much longer 5 per cent.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Does the minister feel that with this clause in the Act stating the exact terms of the agreement, the board will have power to make an agreement containing the condition that there shall be no cash payment for the first or second year on account of principal; so that people will not be .put in default where, in the opinion of the board, they cannot possibly meet the payment?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
We have not that power and personally I would not have that power. The soldier knows what he is confronting.



1	think it is better to have him know that he must commence paying back at once. If it is not his fault, and he is doing his duty, his time will be extended, but he must understand that he must do his duty and take care of his obligations. I want them all to understand that and n t merely some of them. I know there will be a class to be treated differently from the rest because their land is not immediately productive in the sense that lands of others are but the agreements will all have to be the same.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: The committee will be pleased to know that in the Vancouver office we had cases of men who had mapped out their course for the next few years and who were able to show to the satisfaction of the board exactly how, where, and from what sources they expected to raise the revenue that would be required to meet their obligations. They had gone to the trouble of preparing a statement to convince the board that they could meet their obligations even from the first year. The men are not regardless of the fact that they must pay their obligations even from the very first and those who are entering upon highly improved land fully expect to begin paying at the end of the first year.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
You are asking these men to sign something that it is physically impossible to carry out. Men on new land cannot make their payment the first year. The men are being asked to undertake to do something that the board knows it is physically impossible to do.
On section 17-(1) calculation of price by board; (2) improvements to be considered :

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
In regard to subsection
2	of clause 17, is it the intention of the board to make improvements to land they are holding?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Yes, the board has full power to do it but we do not do so as a matter of practice. We have never launched upon that yet. I doubt if we ever will because it involves the buying of land before we have a purchaser for it and we want to avoid that. We might have to do so if we were buying a block of land; we might get it much more cheaply by taking it all. Subsection 2 of section 17 contemplates that possibility and provides accordingly.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: What is the nature of the improvements that you contemplate malt' ing?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
If we bought a block
of land there might be some portion of it that we would have to clear to enable a man to commence farming at once.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: While in Australia I found something of that kind in connection with the Victoria Government's scheme for providing land for settlement. They would take over a block of land and improve it by constructing roads, drainage, fences and even houses before they would even undertake to sell it. I would like to ask the minister if there is any intention on the part of the Government to take areas and make them fit for settlement before they are opened up?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
No, that is not the
policy we adopt. If that is done in Australia it is done under the Governments of the States and not under the Federal Government and the same principle should apply here. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has recently done that as a private enterprise and in the case of soldiers settlement the Canadian Pacific has made arrangements with us whereby it discounts its list price to the extent of 20 per cent on land sold to any settler approved under this Act. That is an immense advantage in dealing with all Canadian Pacific lands. That is an arrangement which has been recently made.
On section 18-sales of stock and equipment:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
I would like this to
stand at the request of the War Veterans' Association. They have asked for a rearrangement of subsection 2 to enable the board to loan more than the maximum on the chattels, taking it from the other loan and getting double the sum on chattels so that the board may give up to $4,000 on a stock loan, their idea being to allow the cattle industry to be engaged in by many soldiers who desire to do so. I wish to give further consideration to that before the clause passes.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 2-resale upon default:

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
In the event of a soldier
abandoning his land, what will the process be?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
The board would then
cancel the sale and the land would revest in the board free from all claim whatsoever on the part of the soldier. Then the board would have the power to settle another sol-

dier upon that land taking over the obligations that the man left, but if the board places anybody except a soldier on the land it can only do so with the approval of the minister and the Governor in Council.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Will the board have to get the full price of the land from another soldier?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: They could only sell to some one other than a soldier with the approval of the minister, and they can only sell for anything less than what they have against the land after a full recital of the circumstances by the board and the approval of the Governor in Council. They cannot lose anything on the land except by the approval of the Governor in Council.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: What action do you contemplate against the soldier who has abandoned that land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: He is liable for it, but a judgment against one who abandons land under these circumstances, will, I am afraid, not be of much value.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: You may keep the liability?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: We may keep the liability on the books.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
I am not very familiar with some of the decisions in the courts in the West that have been going further in recognizing equities than we have been in the Eastern provinces. That is where a man enters upon land and pays a certain amount of money for it, and fails, I have read some western decisions in which it is still held that the man was entitled to anything that he has forfeited. That is to say where the land was worth $2,000 and he had paid $1,500, and was unable to pay the balance and had to abandon the land, I notice that the courts, not dealing with the Crown, but in cases involving private individuals, have given some recognition to the rights of the settler, although he was not able to carry out the agreement to the full extent.
I do not know whether the Minister is familiar with these cases or not; possibly the circumstances are different when the man is dealing with the Crown. In this Bill, I observe, the absolute right is taken away.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
The decisions to which my hon. friend refers are of comparatively recent years and do go a long way in the nature of recognizing the equity of redemption and even the payment the man has
made, upon cancellation. They have no relevance now because sub-section 3 wipes them off and declares finally in statutory form that there is no equity in redemption, and there is no right of claim upon the moneys paid. That being done, of course, the courts are quite powerless to enter and pronounce against the authority of Parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: I quite understand that, but my position is as to whether the minister recognizes the fairness of the principles laid down by these decisions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
The King can do no
wrong.

speechtext: Under this Bill, a man that owns his farm, but has an encumbrance against it of more than $2,500, cannot take advantage of this legislation. Would it not be possible for the minister to reconsider that provision?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
The War Veterans Association have pressed upon me a reconsideration of this clause in the direction suggested by my hon. friend. It will be recalled that I stated that as regards the man who owned his land and merely wanted an advance for' the purpose of wiping off encumbrances, we did not feel we ought to do the same as in the case of a man who was purchasing the land to become a settler, because in the latter instance we are adding a new settler, whereas in the former, we are merely exercising the functions of a loan company-we are not doing anything for settlement at all. We do not want to get into that field any more than we can avoid, so we adopted the maximum of $2,500 which was fixed by the 1917 Act s

related to the'man who owns his land. We say: " We will lend you up to that amount and we will lend you for improvements and for stock, hut we will not lend you on your land alone beyond the $2,500 fixed by the 1917 Act merely for the purpose of clearing off encumbrances-that is loan company work." So the man who owns his land can get advances up to $5,500, but only to the extent of $2,500 on the land as then valued. I think that is a fair division to make; in my opinion we ought not to go any further.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. MAH A.RG:	Mr. Chairman, we were
discussing the point as to whether a larger amount than $2,600 should be advanced to pay off a previous loan. I think it is very desirable that this amount should be increased. While the minister states that the primary intention of the Act is to create new settlers, yet I think it is just, as essential to retain the old settlers-in fact, possibly it is just a little more essential. Had we been able to retain all the settlers that went on the land in the past, we would be in a much different position to-day. A number of these men went overseas with loans against their land, and, during their absence at-the front their farms have been more or less neglected in a great many cases. The loan companies are pressing for repayment, and the men are unable to meet the companies' demands. The conditions of these repayments are rather burdensome, the interest almost invariably being 8 per cent, and in some cases even 9 per cent, I am given to understand. I do not think the minister could do better for those men than to increase this advance sufficiently to wipe off encumbrances. It might be increased up .to $3,500, or just as high as the loan to be advanced to the soldier who is purchasing his land.

it would be at all the part of wisdom, though, to put those men on the same level with the men who are actually being placed on the land by the board.

subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Yes, and throughout the Bill there are very many important departures from common law principles; there have to be. This is a task we have assumed for the benefit of the whole Dominion, consequently we must assert for ourselves rights that, ordinarily, are provincial rights, but which we are in a position to assert because the lands become our own. In this regard it is, of course, necessary to obtain a real obligation on the part of the men with whom we are going to deal, and we cannot refuse to deal with a returned soldier because he happens to be under twenty-one years of age; consequently we have to make him liable.

speechtext: What is the meaning of that? Unless the Government has a bill of sale of the stock in the possession of the man who takes advantage of this Act, and that bill of sale is registered, it is hardly fair that his property should not be subject to his debts, the same as any one else's property. speechtext:
That is a fact. But it is not proposed to put the general public in a position to impose upon that man obligations which may result in his being sold out and in the whole purpose of the Act, which is to make that man a settler, defeated. By this Act we give notice to the public that these special precautions are thrown round that settler; the public must deal with him accordingly. The section says:
Notwithstanding any law, whether statute or otherwise, in force in any province,-
(a)	which authorizes or requires the registration, recording or filing of deeds, mortgages, certificates of judgments, attachments, bills of sale or other documents which effect title to, or evidence the existence of liens or charges upon, property, real, personal or other; or,
(b)	which authorizes the levy upon, or sale under attachment, execution or other process, or the expropriation or seizure of, property, real, personal or other;
unless the board shall otherwise consent in
writing the lands of, or sold by the board to, a settler, and- the live stock and equipment of, or sold by the board to, a settler and the in rease of any such live stock, and the board's an.l the settler's respective interests in such lands, live stock and equipment, shall, for so long as any part of the sale price, or the amount of any advance made with respect to any such property, or any interest, or any amount charged upon such property or any thereof in favour of the board, remains unpaid to the board, be exempt from and not within the operation of such laws.
That is to say, no man can sell the property of that settler, which we provided him with, under execution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: When a private individual lends money and takes as security therefor a bill of sale on the goods and chattels of the person to whom he makes the loan, that bill of sale is registered; the same should be true in the case of loans made by the Government. The merchants of Saskatchewan and Manitoba will not read this Act, and when they see one of these settlers with a fine farm and good stock and equipment they may be willing to extend to him a credit of two or three hundred dollars; but when they come to look for their money they find that they cannot touch his property. When the Government undertake to lend money on security they should comply with the provincial law in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: We cannot adopt that policy, because in some of the provinces there is no provision for registration. These animals that we are providing the settler with are our own, and they still remain our own after they are sold to the settler. There is no provision for registration in Manitoba. If A sells to B in Manitoba certain goods and takes what is known there as a lien note for them, he does not have to register that lien note. Any one dealing with B as to these goods must look up the chain of title; that obligation is on him. In our case we are adopting the policy of identifying our animals so that any one can see that they are the property of the board; and that will be a warning to all concerned. It is manifest that we should not start this man out and then permit others who may be shrewder than he is to defeat the whole purpose of the Bill by selling him enough goods, or in some way getting his obligation, taking execution. The Government must see this man through from beginning to end.

speechtext: In our province the presumption of ownership goes with possession; but before you go too far with the presumption you look up the registry of deeds, and if there is nothing on file there in regard to the property concerned, you have a right to suppose that it is the property of the person who holds it in possession. In Nova Scotia you cannot be safe in following any other course unless there is some agreement to the contrary. There is a pernicious system with respect to the sale of pianos, organs and that sort of thing which is creating havoc in our province because of the fact that the paper which is taken by way of security is not put on file; but apart from that, everything has to be dealt with under the Bill of Sale Act.

speechtext: It may be a good thing for the Government to put a man on 100 or 150 acres of land, well stocked and equipped, and to protect him so that he can defy the public, but it seems to me that it does not tend to improve the moral standing of the man who goes on the land.

We purchase the goods and sell them to these men, and we have a system of stamping them in such a way that any one on investigation can see they are ours. What

we hold out to the whole country is this warning that every man in the district will know who is a soldier settler. It will not be very long until they get to know that as regards that soldier settler a special law exists, and they must take care in dealing with him not to rely for security on goods to that soldier by the Government. I do not think there will be any difficulty; there has not been so far, and this has been in effect since the 11th oif February, and has worked very well.

speechtext: I believe this will create a dangerous situation for the mercantile and professional interests. Any person wishing ito do business with a soldier settler would take it for granted that his security was gilt-edged, because there would: be nothing on record in the registry office to show to the contrary, and I do not know by what means they would trace up the settler's standing. I fail to see any reason why the Government should not register the documents which affeot the title to the property. Why should it not be placed on record in the registry office in the various provinces? I think that would be in the interest of the settler as well, because if there is any doubt in the mind of the general public as to his general stability or title to the property it would affect the settler prejudicially. I certainly think it would be in the interest both of the settler and of the mercantile and professional interests to have some system of registration whereby the exact title could be ascertained by those desiring to know.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
I think that the hon. member ought to take special pains to see that no merchant is under any apprehension in that regard, because the board is absolutely determined that it is not going to undertake these obligations as trustee for the public, and expose the settler to exhibiting the Government's goods as the basis of the credit to him. The board has received ample warning in this regard. There is evidence abundant that myriads of people were simply hanging by the wayside waiting for this scheme to come into operation, expecting that they would be the real beneficiaries thereby. Why, we have cases, and more than one, of agents who have sold a cream separator to a sol-

dier with, one cow, and these things will continue unless we take some special precautions. What is the difficulty about a merchant knowing? It is not hard for him to find out, if he is dealing with a soldier settler, that he cannot rely for his security on the goods the Government provides. If the man is reliable he can give him credit if he wishes, but he had better not rely for his security on the goods that we supply to that man There is no difficulty about them knowing the law in that regard, and if they do not know it, they had better inquire and find out. In my judgment, the whole plan would be doomed to inevitable failure on any other basis whatsoever.

speechtext: I fail to realize that by showing the man's standing you would be creating a basis for credit. I think it would have just the reverse effect; it would protect the general public. It would also be protecting the Government's interest. I do not see why the Government should make laws to govern private individuals, and not live up to those laws themselves, as in this case. I think the Government should live up to the law just the same as any individual in the country.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.

under this Act acquire Canadian Pacifie Railway lands?

subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.

Yes. They are just
the same as any other. maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: When the board has acquired the Canadian Pacific lands will those lands then become liable to taxation?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: They would not if the board held them because the board represents His Majesty, and at common law His Majesty cannot be taxed. But the board does not acquire them until it sells them. The hoard finds the
settler first. As soon as the prospective settler selects the land, the board sends out one of its inspectors and if the price is found to be right the board buys tSe land and the sale to the settler is carried on simultaneously.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.

In case land now liable for
taxation is taken over by the board and is

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: No, the interest of the board could not be taken under tax sale. But we realize the necessity of not undermining the municipality. That is going to be the policy of the board and it will be to their interest to see that the settler's taxes are paid.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: Does this mean that only the interest that the settler has in the land is taxable, or the whole property?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: That is not what I mean. I understand it is proposed that the moment a plan is filed and notice given that title to the land vests in the board, the proceedings described in this 'Section may take place. Yet, the owner may not accept the money, he may want to go to the Exchequer court, and it takes two or three years before the matter is finally settled. In the meantime, there may be an application for a warrant to put the board in possession of the land. That is where the hardship comes in. If s man takes the money for the land he ought to give up the title, but he may be entitled to say that the amount offered is not enough, that the case is in the Exchequer court and that he will not give up possession until it is finally disposed of. Is there any provision for notice to the party in possession of the application being made before the Exchequer court?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: The party, under this Act, always has full notice before the expropriation proceedings are taken and when the attempt is made to purchase the land. They try to come to a friendly arrangement as to the price. If that proves impossible notice of expropriation is given and the filing of the plan follows. . C nave no doubt it will be possible for the board to act harshly in obtaining the title, but the board is not going to do so. At the same time, the board cannot be delayed, out of mere obstinacy, in obtaining possession of the land for the settler. This is not a new law at all; it has been the law for many years and this is the way that possession has been taken in hundreds of thousands of cases of appropriation under such circumstances.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext: I think it is the common practice to give notice. There is nothing better established in British law than that you cannot make an order against a man in the court without giving him notice. The Supreme Court of Canada have held over and over again that a man cannot be bound by any proceedings which take place in court of which he has had no notice. The court may grant an order but the man should have notice before the order is granted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.

There is some advantage to the country in handing land over to somebody who will use it as against the man who will not use it and who holds it for speculative purposes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.

On section 59-power of board to estimate land- apart from buildings and to vary amount as to balance due:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
I desire to propose two amendments to this clause. The way it reads now the board is empowered to take any amount not exceeding $1,000 away from the stock loan and add it to improvements. The amendment I propose is to enable the board to take away from the improvements .loan and add it to the stock loan. The amendment will therefore empower the board to vary the provisions of section 18 in that regard and:
(li) To vary the provisions of section sixteen to nineteen inclusively, of this Act, so that live stock and equipment to a value not exceeding three thousand dollars may he sold to a settler, but so that the total amount of balance of price and advances -remaining unpaid by the settler as the result of the exercise by the board of any of its powers under this Act shall not exceed seven thousand five hundred dollars.
The Bill will then provide that $1,000 may be taken off stock and added to the amount available for improvements, or the stock loan may be raised $1,000 and made $3,000, so long as the total does not exceed $7,500. I think that will be clear to the committee. That is to meet the strong representations made by the war veterans that we were not adequately providing for stock ;farming, especially in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I also desire to amend subsection (1) by adding the following subclause (c):
In all cases of sales of orchard or fruit lands, to apply the provisions of section 18 of this Act, with such other provisions thereof as may depend upon or have relation to those of said section, as if for the words "live stock or equipment" or "live stock and equipment acquired under authority of this Act" or words to the same effect in said section or in any of said sections appearing, there were substituted

the words "fruit trees, already planted or growing on any land sold by the board to the settler,"-
That is to say, providing for the substitution of fruit trees already planted or growing on any land sold by the board to the settler.
-and, for any purpose of this Act, to estimate the value of the trees and shruibs already planted or growing on any land being sold by the board to the settler apart from the value of such land.
I submit that the better course would be to have this amendment as proposed printed in Hansard, and to let the clause stand, so that the members of the committee may see the clause in the morning as it will appear in its amended form, and we can deal with it when we are in committee again on the Bill. It makes a very substantial amendment to section 59.

Section stands.
On section 61-No fee or commission on any sale to board:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: BILL TO ASSIST SETTLEMENT OF RETURNED SOLDIERS UPON THE LAND.
speechtext:
This is a very important clause. It provides that:
(1)	No person, firm or corporation shall be entitled to charge or to collect as against or from any other person, firm or corporation any fee or commission or advance of price for services rendered in the sale of any land made to the board, whether for the finding or introducing of a buyer or otherwise.
(2)	No person, firm or corporation shall pay to any other person, firm or corporation any such fee or commission or advance of price for any such services.
(3)	The board may require of any person, firm or corporation from whom It purchases land, or who is in any manner interested therein, the execution of an affidavit in Form E in the Schedule to this Act.
The affidavit contains a declaration that no commission whatever is paid in connection with the transaction. It must not be inferred because this clause is inserted that the business of a commission land agent is wrongful, or criminal, or any less legitimate than any other business. But the fact is that owing to its being the Government that is purchasing and dealing with these lands, the necessity for shutting out even access to fraud is so great that we deem it best to prohibit commissions altogether. In fact, we do not know any other way of doing it. The Government when purchasing land in a locality does not know every individual resident there, and it is very difficult for the Government, as for a private individual,
to guard itself against being imposed on in this way. Consequently we provide that no commission shall be charged on any sale of land to the board.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
In subsection 2,
what "census" is referred to?-the federal census that is taken every ten years? Or would that include also the interim census taken from time to time in the western provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
