speechtext:
I am not discussing that principle. I am dealing with the expenditure of money on roads, which I say are a
great asset to the country, and I hope the Bill will go through. I think it was a mistake, when a similar Bill was introduced into the House years ago, that it did not go through. If it had passed we would have been in a better financial position to-day.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: What is meant by " main highways?" The question was asked by an hon. gentleman on the other side whether the money will be used on the main highway, and the minister said, no. The minister was then asked about some apprehended danger that the location, of the road would be dictated by the Federal Government and he said it would not, nor would the local government ...cate where the road should be constructed; he said it would be a matter of agreement. This is at once a matter for consolation and fear. If no one is going to determine where the road is to be there will be nothing to quarrel about, but we may be left without a road at all. What does the minister mean by " main highway?"

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The local governments, most of which have highways departments, have divided roads into three classes. One class comprises roads that run to market towns. These are kept up by the municipalities and carry a little more than the traffic created by the farmers along the road. The second class of roads radiate from local markets or shipping points and carry a considerable accumulation of traffic, such roads as those leading into Ottawa or Montreal, for instance. Then there are the main highways between important cities and towns and other terminal points. A road between Montreal and Toronto would be a main highway. In some of the new provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan, for instance, a city or town might not want to see all the money spent in building one main road through the centre of the province. In Saskatchewan there are large market centres where there must be market roads, and they would likely want to divide up their money on these several roads, while Ontario might want to run a main road from Montreal to Toronto. But the Dominion and Provincial Governments will have to agree as to where it would be best to lay out roads. After it is decided where the roads will be built the Dominion Government will authorize the provinces to expend the money, we reserving the right to have our inspectors see the work carried out in accordance with the specifications and the contract awarded, for which of course public tenders will be called.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: Assuming that there has been correspondence with the Provincial Governments, what stand do they take in regard to receiving the money, and what governments can the minister speak of with certainty?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
The representatives of several governments have been here consulting with me and some of them took this position:	We want to divide this
money up among the principal roads leading into these different centres, but we do not want to expend our money in running these roads right through.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
What governments?
Mr. J. D. REID' We have had representatives from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, and Ontario, and some of the western provinces-I think, Manitoba, British Columbia and Alberta.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
Are they favourable to
the scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: Yes, every one of them is urging it forward and looking for these highways.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
Is the Dominion
Government insisting on one, if not two, roads being built across the province of British Columbia and in the Lake Superior district ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The provincial government are building roads in- netv Ontario from Port Arthur east. A lot of this money would go into that if they wished to expend it in that way. The roads that they are constructing in new Ontario are doing a great deal of good, and the Ontario government want to spend all the money they can in opening up new Ontario and extending roads on up through that territory towards Port Arthur. It is a new country and it is very costly to build roads up the-e.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
I do not know that I can add anything to this discussion but I would not want the vote to be taken without expressing the view of the district from which I come which is that there is virtue in this legislation. Practically the roads that exist in the county of Frontenac, the city of Kingston and the adjacent counties, were built for vehicular traffic and are not sufficiently well built to stand the stress and strain of the 'highpowered car, and certainly are not useful for early spring or late autumn traffic. A year or two ago it was my privilege to go around lake Ontario by

motor and I could not help noticing the very advantageous condition that existed in New York state. From the time you leave Ontario at Prescott or Brockville until you again get into Ontario at Niagara Falls the Toads in the main are as smooth as a table, and in whichever direction traffic is moving you are impressed by the tremendous loads that are taken to market by motor as compared with the small loads that are hauled in our part of the country. Not only that, but the whole of the New York state is alive with tourist traffic, to a certain extent, going from the province of Ontario and the country that lies north of the American border. But the moment you get into Ontario the bad roads are a deterrent, and as you go along there is one cause of complaint to the American tourists and that is that the roads are not suitable for tourist traffic. Every one tells you the same story: "This is the last time I am coming to Ontario until you give us better roads." They admit our scenery is good, they admit there is much that we have to offer to bring them into Canada, but they are indisposed to risk their cars in going over our roads which are unsuitable for them. There is another change that has taken place. Practically every farmer, if he does not now own a motor car is aspiring to, and to get the best use from it he wants to be able to use it in early spring and late fall. That is practically impossible if something further cannot be done to improve our roads. I know that Ontario has spent the province's money and that municipalities have contributed largely, but there is not sufficient money, unless outside aid is given, to link up the improved roads that have been built. I hope this House will see its way to give support to this appropriation so that we may have continued progress in this direction.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The hon. member says "unless outside aid is given." Where do you expect the money to come from unless you borrow it, for which the people of Ontario will have to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
I expect we will get the money where we got the money for building the railways in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
(Mr. M. CLARK: Building railways is a Dominion work, whereas, according to what we hear from lawyers, this is a provincial work.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: I do not understand that railways are wholly a Dominion concern. There are railways being built by the provinces themselves and by corporations that are incorporated by the provincial legislatures. Therefore, the building of railways is not entirely under- Dominion jurisdiction. We are giving aid to the provinces in connection with other matters which are entirely under their jurisdiction. In the matter of education we are giving them aid, and we are also keeping partial control. We are asking that we be allowed to supervise the expenditures in order to see that the money is spent in accordance with the money voted by Parliament. That is all that we are doing in this case.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The minister says that we are building railways. If I am informed rightly the provinces which are building these railways own their own natural resources.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: How much money does the minister propose spending this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: That would depend entirely on what the provinces would be willing to spend. If the provinces say they are willing to proceed with highways and to press them forward, of course, we would have to pay 40 per cent of what they would expend. If they do not wish to proceed with the construction, we would not have to pay any of the money.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: Has the minister an actual understanding with any one of the provinces that they are willing to embark upon an expenditure on the basis of the Dominion contributing 40 per cent and the province 60 per cent, particularly with the province of Nova Scotia?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext: The Provincial Government of Nova Scotia are anxious that we proceed with this Bill, and the information they give me is that they are willing to put up the 60 per cent and to accept the 40 per cent given by the Dominion of Canada and proceed with the construction of highways.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The minister is going to bring in a Bill on this resolution, I understand?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
The resolution states that $80,000 is to be apportioned to each of the provinces. That will be $720,000 per annum. That will be $3,600,000 in the course of five years, and in addition $400,000 is to be distributed among the provinces according to population. This amount of $80,000, if I understand rightly, will have to be expended within five years to give the provinces the right to the benefit of it. If one province fails to disburse the required amount, or to construct roads to the extent of 60 per cent of the amount of the $80,000, what will be done with the remainder of the money? Supposing the province of Quebec does not construct $400,000 worth of roads in order to make up the 60 per cent, what will happen? It would have to construct $600,000 worth of roads in order to get $400,000.
What will be done with the excess if say only $200,000 out of $300,000 of the Federal Government's money is expended, and how will that balance be apportioned? If I understand the facts rightly, the accounts will be closed at the end of five years and in the case of any province which has not complied with the requirements its share of the federal grant will remain unexpended. Now, will this balance be apportioned among the other provinces or will it go back to the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Mr_ J. D. REID: The honourable member is supposing something which, I think, will never occur. The representatives of the different provincial governments have been in Ottawa conferring with the Minister of Railways, and from the discussion I have had with them they are all anxious for the construction of good roads. Their desire is to improve the existing roads and construct new highways-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: Does the minister admit that what I have said is possible?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: -and, therefore, in my opinion, the money will be all used: I think I can say that because I have discussed the matter with the representatives of practically all the provinces. Of course, if any province does not accept the grant it would still remain in the Consolidated Revenue Fund, but that is a point in the Bill which has not been provided for. When the Bill comes up for second reading I will consider the suggestion which my honourable friend has made. I would much prefer that the provinces go ahead with the construction of good roads because in my opinion nothing will be more advantageous to them. The amount proposed to be voted is not very large, but I have not the slightest doubt but that every province will avail itself of the proportion to which it will be entitled under this Bill.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.

If the money is not used this year it will doubtless be taken advantage of in the year following.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: That is all very well, but aJt the end of five years some of this money may be unexpended and it should be taken advantage of by those provinces which show themselves enterprising and progressive. That is what I want to provide for.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: We will give it to Quebec.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has no cause to laugh at Quebec which is far ahead of British Columbia, or any other province, in the matter of good roads. I can drive my hon. friend all through the province of Quebec on as good a road as he can show me anywhere either in the neighbouring Republic or in British Columbia. If this legislation were to be based on aggressiveness and enterprise in the matter of good roads, the hon. gentleman can depend upon it we would wear the feather in our cap.
The resolution sets forth that the expenditure must be forty per cent of the amount which, " in the opinion of the minister, is actually necessary and reasonable in the cost of construction or improvement of such highway." In such a matter it is not the opinion of the minister that I, as a member of Parliament would like to have, but the figures and vouchers of the Provincial Governments. What I would suggest is that the actual cost of the road be determined by engineers and by provincial vouchers showing that the money has actually been paid out, and I will move an amendment to that effect when the Bill is introduced.
Mr. OAHIiLL: I hate to detain the House at this late hour but my constituents are very much interested in good roads, and have asked me to ascertain from the Government whether they can or cannot get any part of this money for the improvement of the existing roads, or the construction of new highways, and that I have been endeavouring to do. I asked the (Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) with respect to it, and I must say that I am somewhat at a loss to know whether my constituency was going to benefit by the expenditure of this money or not. When the resolution was before the committee on a previous occasion the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) made a definite statement that no portion of it would be spent except on main highways to leading centres. Now the Minister of Railways says it will be a matter of agreement between the Provincial Governments and the Dominion authority. The people in my constituency apparently seem to realize more than some hon. gentlemen do that they must be responsible for their share of this money, and that any constituencies that fail to receive any portion of it will be helping to build roads in other localities. The people in my constituency are building roads and want to continue to do so, but they do not feel that they are in a position to put their hands in their pockets and contribute

money for the building of roads in British Columbia while they still need roads in Pontiac county: If this money were to be expended on any road to which the provincial government would give a grant so that the back townships would also profit by it, as well as the main highways, I would not be so strongly opposed to it. My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) talks of automobiles and' tourists, but I want to tell him that there are hundreds and thousands of farmers in this country that have not got any kind of tourist road to travel on and are struggling to build roads to their market towns. They are anxious to get money for this purpose, but they are not keen on the question of devoting money voted by this Parliament for the construction of highways in the interests of automobile tourists at the sacrifice of their own roads. 1 must say I am strongly opposed to so much paternalism on the part of this Government towards the provinces. First, they started with aid for agriculture-with a string attached to it; then aid for technical education-with a string attached to it; next the housebuilding programme-with a string attached to it; and now we have this roadbuilding scheme-also with a string attached. If the provinces want this money, why not give it as a subsidy? The very same people that elect representatives to the provincial legislature also elect the representatives in this House.
I have no doubt that they elect just as honest men to the local legislatures as they do to the Federal House, and these men can be trusted to spend the money in the provinces. If the Dominion Government has a surplus of funds and feel that the provinces are entitled to some of the surplus, let it make grants to the provinces outright, the money to be used on roads or on technical education and other things. They are just as capable of looking after the expenditure as is the Dominion Government. So, Mr. Chairman, if the minister will not withdraw his Bill, I say to him: Give this money to the provinces without any strings on it, to be spent on a certain pro rata basis. Then I do not think there would be so much objection to the Bill. But I am afraid there will be great objection to it by members representing constituencies where they need roads, but will not be able to benefit by these grants, particularly in the rural districts. The city districts,-where you are going to run a road between Montreal and Toronto-might naturally favour the proposal, I do not doubt they will; in fact, I think some
hon. members on both sides of the House expect the road to run 'through their constituencies. But when you talk of the provinces getting "found" money from the Dominion Government, it is no such thing. The people of 'Canada must supply this money, and the unfortunate part of it is, as my hon. friend from Bed Deer would say, in the method of collecting it the Government collects two or three dollars from the tax payer for the one dollar that gets into the Treasury. Leave the roads to the provinces. We are quite satisfied in Quebec to build our own roads, and we are doing the work to-day. My hon. friend says that he cannot get on any good roads outside the province of Ontario. If he will build good roads to the borders of my province, he will get on good roads when he passes the provincial boundary. The Prairie Provinces have a fair system of dirt roads that apparently suits them very well. British Columbia may need higher priced roads, and if they do they have the material to build them. But we know that the only people interested in these grants, are those who think they are getting free money in some constituency through which roads could be arranged to be built.
Some hon. M'EMfBEBS: Carried,

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
I do not often inflict
my utterances upon this House, and a good many of the hon. gentlemen who are so vociferously shouting "carried", evidently with the intention to prevent me from speaking, are the same gentlemen to whom I have listened with a great deal of tedium on various occasions, and I expect to do so again. I think this debate has been exceedingly illuminating, but there is a good deal of mental darkness still prevailing upon the subject. I hear one member stating that he is supporting this resolution because he is ir. favour of a transcontinental highway. Thereupon the minister says that it is not the purpose of the Government to build a transcontinental highway, that the kind of roads to foe fouilt are interurban and country roads. Then another gentleman says that he favours the proposition because he wants the same kind of roads that exist in the United States. Everybody knows that the roads of the United States are built by the state legislatures and are permanent roads. I would like to ask the minister if that is the kind of road he proposes to have built with the money which is provided for by this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: In each case we would have to take the matter up with the Provincial Government and find out exactly what their proposition is. Some of the provinces might prefer spending the money on macadamized roads and distributing it over a longer distance, while other provinces, for instance, the province of Ontario, as I stated, might want to build permanent roads similar to those in New York state, which would cost probably from $8,000 to $10,000 a mile. Or they might say they would expend part of the money that way and part in macadamized roads, and we might agree to that. Probably in the Prairie Provinces they would not want to spend the money, I would take it for granted, on a road right through each province at probably from $8,000 to $10,000 a mile, they would want a different kind of road entirely from that desired by the Ontario Government. So it would all depend on the proposition put up by the Provincial Governments as to whether it would be a macadamized or a concrete road or some other kind of road. In the West, there must be many roads required, and they could not possibly he expected to spend the money on very expensive roads; whereas in Ontario we would probably build roads of a more permanent character than those in the West.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: I am very much indebted to the hon. minister for his courtesy in answering my question, but with all deference to him I am inclined to the opinion that he is quite as much in the dark about this matter as the other members of the House; and with all deference again, it seems to me before we embark on so vast a scheme we ought not to have such misty ideas, but we ought to have a clear-cut, definite policy. However, I am going to ask for some information in another direction. I would like to know if. the minister has any information as to the systems of roadbuilding employed by the different provincial governments who would have the expending of the money provided for by this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
Several of the provinces have commissions for the construction of roads, and they engage the very best men they can get-men who are experts on the subject of road building. The work is carried on in that way in the province of Ontario and in the province of Quebec. I do not know whether they have such a commission in the province of Nova Scotia in which the constituency of the hon. member (Mr. Davidson) is situated. I believe this

is going to be a very important matter for the rural population, and they are insisting on good roads. In the province of Ontario about 109,000 automobile licenses were issued last year, and over half of those were issued to the rural districts. In the province of Saskatchewan there were practically 40,000 licenses taken out, the next largest number, and they would be almost entirely rural I should say. I merely mention that to show the growth of motor traffic with the farmers. There is not a large city to-day but its market is crowded with motors from the country, and they come from very long distances.
A few years ago the farmers of my own constituency had to ship everything by rail; since motor cars have come into common use, they marketed their goods in Ottawa, and even in Montreal. Moreover the farmers can go to the large centres during nine months of the year instead of during only five or six. Good roads are a benefit to the rural population in that the services of physicians are made more available to the people; where the roads are bad, perhaps impassable, even where telephones are available a doctor may find it impossible to answer a call, or at least to answer it promptly.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
Should any intelligent
elector take the trouble, which I very much doubt, to pursue the windings of this debate I am perfectly certain that he will find himself in a state of mind akin to that which the member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) has described as his. If we are to vote on this thing I think we should vote intelligently. Now, what are the propositions of a concrete nature that have, been put before us in support of this resolution? The minister mentioned the providing of work for returned soldiers, and in the next breath he expressed very great doubt whether any soldiers would want the work. Well, that does not seem to be a very sound basis upon which to build a case for the expenditure of $20,000,000. I want to point out to the minister and to the Government that the further they go along the line of spending money upon what is non-productive work, the further they will produce people who want that non-productive work, and the more people they take out of the work of production the more they will put the cost of living up in this country. That is one of the objects which has been mentioned by the minister himself. The member for West Kootenay (Mr. Green) talked of building a transcontinental highway. I

cannot think that he was serious. What would $20,000,000 do towards the building of such a highway if it were all expended upon that one proposition? It would scarcely touch the scheme. So we may dismiss that; I assume that not a cent of this would go towards the building of 'a transcontinental highway, even if the money were voted now.
Then, the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) with truly democratic instinct, puts up the case of the American tourist as a reason why the highly-taxed people of this country should be enthusiastic over this road ischeme. Well, I should like to see the road leading into his constituency from the United States come as rapidly as possible to the excellence of the State roads- though eight millions of people with a larger territory to build roads upon can hardly be expected to equal the work of 110,000,000 upon a smaller territory, especially in view of the fact that we are strained by the expenditures of a war in which we entered three years before the United States did. But the point I want to put to this Committee is, if we are going to spend this money upon the building of roads connecting the United States with Canada, then we cannot spend it on a national highway.
Then, my hon. friend (Mr. Sexsmith) says that the scheme is really to help the farmers to get their stuff to market around the little local towns and so reduce the cost of living. What a very confiding Committee we shall be if we vote for this scheme put forward along these various lines or supported by these various arguments. If the minister is really serious in his intentions to press this scheme, I hope that when he speaks again, if he intends to speak again, he will tell us what he really wants this money for. Is he in favour of a national highway, and is any of this money to go to that? We have a right to know, because one of the gentlemen sitting behind him evidently has that in his mind. Or is he in favour of the highly-taxed citizens of this country looking particularly after the needs of American tourists? If that is what is in the minister's mind; if that is what is behind this proposal, then I should like to know, and my farmers would like to know it. If it is to give work to the returned soldiers-to which, incidentally, returned soldiers will not go, according to the minister-then I should also like that reason to give to my electors. If it is to help the farmers and to reduce the cost of living, then I should
be in the position of my friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill); I should, with all modesty, want to know how much of it is actually going to the constituency of Bed Deer. I must say that I do not like to complain of the minister's statements, but it is no wonder they were hazy if he had in mind the various explanations which have been given by other supporters of the scheme; because it would pass the combined eloquence and clarity of Demosthenes and Cicero to combine and reconcile these schemes-and nobody will charge the minister with being in the same class as Demosthenes and Cicero.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
I stated that for several reasons I wanted this Bill to be passed this session. One was to provide work for returned soldiers; I believe that if this scheme is put through it will provide work during the next two or three or four years for very many of our men who have returned from the front, and for whom we might not be able to find other employment. I believe that nothing will reduce the cost of living more than the passing of this Bill and the building up of good roads throughout Canada. If you have good roads, men are encouraged to go on the farm and immigration is encouraged; and if you can get more people on the farm and thereby increase production, you certainly reduce the cost of living. I believe that the building of good roads increases the value of the rural properties through which they run; nothing will add more to the comfort of the rural population than good roads. One of the greatest benefits resulting to the rural population from the building of good roads is that of their being able to get a physician at any time; this would not be possible now in the spring and fall fn oases where the roads were very bad. As to the question of tourists, I do not suggest that this money be spent entirely upon the building of roads for the accommodation of tourist traffic, but I do say that if, in addition to the advantages that I have mentioned, we oan, by encouraging good roads, increase the tourist traffic throughout our country, we are doing something which is of very great value. I have here a statement which will indicate the value of tourist traffic in other countries which have good roads.	,
The amount annually expended by tourists is estimated as follows: France, $500,000,000; Switzerland, $150,000,000; Italy, $100,000,000; Maine, $40,000,000; Americans in England,. $25,000,000; Americans abroad, $350,000,000. Hon. members need only go to any of our summer resorts in Ontario, or any other

province, and see the Americans there, to form some idea of the amount of money that is expended by American tourists in our country. They will then come to the conclusion that the tourist traffic is certainly of some advantage, and I believe of very great advantage to Canada, and nothing but good roads will bring tourists in large numbers.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The Governor of Maine stated last year that the revenue from the tourist trade for that state was five times greater than its lumber revenue had ever been.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: What steps have the Government already taken in the direction of good roads? I believe that some expenditure is now being made by the Dominion Government, looking towards the improvement of highways.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The only thing we have done is this: We have appointed Mr. Campbell, who has had a great deal of experience in the construction of highways, as commissioner. He has a small staff, and is trying to get an organization together to look after the matter of specifications. He is also studying the localities in which he thinks the roads should be constructed. A small vote of $25,000 was passed by the House this session, and it is out of this vote that this work is being done. I cannot expend anything under this Bill until it becomes law.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: In what department does Mr; Campbell work?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: He is in the Department of Railways and Canals. We have expended only a portion of the $25,000 vote.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: Is it not true that the Mines Department is working along this line?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: No, the only expenditure they are making is in connection with the inspection of mining areas in the different provinces.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
I have listened very
patiently to this discussion on the national highway project, but as yet I am unable to understand whether it is to be a national highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific or a system of local roads throughout th# provinces. If the minister would take us into his confidence, and tell us that it was to be a national highway I would be opposed to it., I cannot see how such a road is going to reduce the cost of living. I am of the opinion that if you want to

reduce the cost of living it would be much better to spend this amount of money in railway branch lines, especially in the West, where we have thousands of farmers living forty and fifty and sixty miles beyond the national railway system, raising wheat and paying forty-five and fifty cents per bushel for hauling it to the railway. The minister must know that this condition cannot exist when prices come down to normal, and if those farmers living up there stop producing wheat when the price drops, naturally the amount of wheat produced will be diminished. I think it would be much better to drop this project of a national highway for the meantime, and construct branch lines of railway to the settlers who are now living fifty and sixty and seventy miles beyond the railway. Our returned soldiers are going in there to-day by the thousands, as far as eighty miles back from the railway. Are we not going to help them to get their products to market? It matters not to us, I think, whether our friends, the Yanks to the South, have good roads or not. They have 110,000,000 people to build their roads. Can Canada with only 8,000,000 people be expected to have roads equally as good as those on the other side? I think not. Not only does the production of wheat make more wheat products, but there are also the by-products to consider, which are used in the feeding of hogs and cattle, and all this helps to reduce the cost of living. I would ask the minister to consider this matter seriously and withdraw the Bill for the present, until he can lay down a definite policy and tell us just exactly what this scheme is to be. I am sorry, but if this comes to a vote I shall be compelled to vote against it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: I am desirous of speaking at some length on this resolution, and inasmuch as it is now rather late and we have done a full day's work, I would ask the minister if he would consent to have the committee rise and report progress. Other hon. members whose opinions I am sure would be valued by this committee are also desirous of participating in this debate, and they would be able to be in their places tomorrow and contribute to the discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
I asked the committee to pass this, resolution to-night so that I could get the Bill printed. My hon. friend will have an opportunity of speaking on the second reading of the Bill and again at the committee stage, when he will have the Bill before him. I should like the resolu-

tion to go through to-night if the committee are agreeable.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: I think that this discussion, while, perhaps, not as definite as it might have been, and while many different opinions have been expressed as to just what the resolution means, has on the whole been enlightening, and might with profit be continued. The very fact that there seems to be such a difference of opinion would lead me to believe that. I should like very much to discuss this resolution at this stage, but at this hour of the night I do not wish to inflict a long speech on the House.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: It is cooler now than it will be to-morrow.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
The suggestion made
by the hon. member (Mr. Copp) that it is cooler now is apt. We are just in the proper mood now for legislating on this matter. We are in a receptive frame of mind and are ready for the speech which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davidson) wishes to give us. We are accustomed to late hours and this is an opportune time for the hon. member for Annapolis to follow up the questions he has been hurling at us by the speech which he is anxious to deliver and which I am sure will be quite illuminating. The questions which the hon. member has asked are extremely interesting and give evidence of his possession of quite a fund of information which the Committee is now prepared to receive. I would strongly oppose the suggestion that the Committee should rise and report progress because this is an eminently favourable opportunity for us to get the information which we need in order to help us make progress. Will the hon. member for Annapolis now get up and favour us with some information from that vast fund of knowledge which he possesses, coming as he does from the Maritime Provinces? They do not need good roads there, but nevertheless he has a remarkable interest in the whole subject and is evidently desirous of doing the right thing. I for one am prepared to sit here at least another hour and listen to the information which I know he has bottled up in his brain and is extremely anxious to give to the Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
Notwithstanding the pressing invitation of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) I am inclined to agree to the suggestion that the Committee report progress, in view of the lateness of the hour. If the hon. member for Annapolis desires further discussion of the subject he will have ample
opportunity on the second reading of the Bill. On the second reading hon. members may thoroughly discuss the principles of the Bill, the details of which can be minutely considered in Committee. I think the proposal of the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) therefore, at this stage, after a long day, is a very reasonable one. It must be borne in mind that some of us must get back to work at 11 o'clock, and that we shall have to stay at it until twelve o'clock at night, repeating the same thing the day following, and the day after that. If we are to get the work of the session done we must all look upon a situation of this kind in a reasonable way, and in order to expedite the work I suggest that unless there is some, grave reason to the contrary the proposaf , of the Minister of Railways be carried out and we be allowed to go home.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
May I be allowed to say a few words? If I were in the habit of speaking as frequently as the hon. member for Frontenac I could take a chance with my audience. The hon. gentleman who has -so kindly referred to the enjoyment which he anticipaies from my speech frequently addresses the House. Sometimes I have been driven to the painful necessity of using strenuous efforts to keep a quorum while certain speeches are being made, and I can understand the position of one who does not frequently speak if he were to attempt to occupy very much of the time of the Committee at this hour of the night on a question of this kind. It is rather unusual for me to speak in this House and I am anxious1 to select a time when the hon. gentleman is not obsessed with any great desire for his downy couch and when he can give undivided attention to the affairs of State and matters of first importance. This is a very important subject.
It has not to do with some little appointment to the Kingston penitentiary or any trivial matter of that kind. It has not to do with the vexed provincial question of national schools. It is of supreme importance whether we shall embark on a brand new policy in this country and I think the whole question should be seriously considered. If the minister insists, I shall of course, as I have done before, bow rwith all deference to his wishes and proceed to-night, in my exhausted condition, with the remarks which I intend to make. Looking upon the jaded faces opposite me, I am sure that hon. members will be in a better condition to hear me at a more seasonable time. If it is thought necessary I

will speak to-night, hut I would very much prefer to speak to-morrow.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: I thought, when the hon. member rose, that he was about to give us of the store of information which I know he has in abundance. Possibly I have spoken more frequently than the member for Annapolis and in that respect the House has less to forgive him than me. The hon. mentber has referred to -one or two matters which have nothing to do with this Bill, and since he has wandered afield I presume I may follow him. I have heard the hon. member give some reasons why he is opposed to this Bill. It is not because he does not believe in good roads.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: How does the hon. member know I am' opposed to the Bill? I have not expressed an opinion on the matter.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: If the member has not expressed an opinion he has had an opportunity of doing so, and his whole attitude has been one of opposition. He has expressed himself outside the Chamber, and if he will be as candid in the Chamber as out of it he will say that his reason for opposing the Bill is that he objects to placing money in the hands of the people of Nova Scotia, who, he has said, will use it absolutely for political purposes. If $40 out of $100 is handed to the Government of Nova Scotia, that government, in his opinion, is composed of such a lot of black legs that it will use the money absolutely for political purposes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is misquoting me entirely I never made any such statement and I ask him to withdraw it. i

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
The hon. member did not say "blacklegs", and I withdraw the statement to that extent, but he has come as close to it as he could by inference without using that particular word. If that is his reason for opposing this Biill in the House, as it has been his expressed and only reason out of the House, why is he not candid enough to admit it? He does not, because he knows that an argument of that kind will not appeal to the committee. I repeat that he has frequently outside of the Chamber, used as an argument against the Government voting the money towards the improvement of highways, the alleged fact that if it is placed in the hands of the Government in Nova Scotia, those who are in control of provincial affairs there will use it for party purposes. The hon.
IMr. Davidson.]
member (Mr. J. F. Reid) raises the question about building railroads to farmers 50 or 60 miles away. It is all right, from his point of view, to take the money of the country to build .a steel road for farmers to get produce to market, but it is absolutely illogical from his standpoint to take the money to build a highway for the same purpose.
Why is it that every member for Saskatchewan approves of spending millions of dollars to build the Hudson Bay railway? Is it for the benefit of Canada? It is for the benefit of the farmers of Saskatchewan and Northern Saskatchewan at that. It is all right from their standpoint to build thousands of miles of railway across the continent for the benefit of 500,000 farmers in Saskatchewan, but where you have a population of 2,500,000 in Ontario you must not spend a cent down here to improve roads. There is nothing consistent in these hon. gentlemen at all. They never ask the question :"Where are you going to get the money?"-when it comes to a question of building the Hudson Bay or some other railway in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, or Alberta. The people who have raised most of the money to build these railways in the West can go on raising most of the money to build railways out there and these gentlemen do not lose any sleep over where the money is to come from, but when it is a case of developing the agricultural districts of Old Canada, which has been the source of supply for building up Western 'Canada, they object. That is not a far-sighted way of looking at the situation. Throughout Ontario the building of highways is the greatest issue that you can bring before the people, and they have a right to come to this Government and ask them to contribute towards the building of these highways.

subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The money to build the Hudson Bay railway has been in the treasury for years and years, and it was obtained from the proceeds of the land sold in Saskatchewan.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Frontenac talks about the members from Saskatchewan taking the money out of the country to build a railway. Does the hon. member not know that Saskatchewan is inside the Dominion of Canada and that we are not taking money out of the country? He tells this Committee what Ontario has done for the West. iMore lands were given away in Western Canada by the Dominion Government than would have built all tlhe

railways in the West. I would like to ask the hon. member for Frontenac about the canals which have been built in Ontario by the Dominion Government-and which do not bring any revenue to the federal treasury-not for the benefit of the people of Canada, but for the benefit of the people of Ontario. There is one close to this city built absolutely for pleasure for the use of the people of Ontario, and, I presume, built by all the people of Canada. He complains about the roads of Ontario needing such an amount of money, and yet he tells us that they have the largest population of any province. They have been building roads in Ontario for sixty or seventy-five years. Why does the hon. member for Frontenac not follow the example of the province of 'Quebec? Let him go down there and learn how to build roads, or better still, get a man from Quebec to tell them how to build roads in Ontario, especially in the constituency of Frontenac? If the hon. gentleman will visit the West we will give him a si>in in an automobile on our own mud roads, and when he gets out he will say he has been over one of the smoothest roads that he ever rode over.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: If the hon. member for Frontenac had waited for the remarks that I had intended to make it would have not have been necessary for him to violate the conduct of a gentleman in attempting to disclose in a public discussion confidential matters. The fact that the hon. gentleman interfered with my argument, by rehearsing a portion of it, seems an added reason why I should be allowed to continue my -remarks and perhaps speak in a more logical manner at another sitting of the committee. 'If the hon. gentleman had let me alone I would have been able to present very many more reasons for my opposition. But I submit that the one reason that in my judgment the Government of Nova iScotia would not expend the money that this Government propose to give them wisely, but that they would waste the money, is a cogent and tangible reason and a reason which J might have no hesitancy in expressing to this committee. 'Since the hon. gentleman has referred to remarks which were made to him in a confidential way, I might perhaps be allowed to refer to remarks which were made by him in a public way in reference to this very resolution. When the resolution was 'last before the House the hon. member for Frontenac stated clearly that he only proposed to support a resolution of this kind upon the understanding that permanent roads and nothing but permanent roads were to be built. Am I correct in stating that?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: No, you are not.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: The error in this respect must be due to the occult way in which my honourable friend speaks or to my limited powers of interpretation.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: It is the latter.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: No doubt it is. I hope my honourable friend will regard this as a public question and permit me to enjoy the same liberty of opinion I have always conceded him, although I happen to disagree with him upon this question, and not cherish any little feeling against an old friend simply because he differs with him on a public question. Do I understand the minister refuses to allow the committee to rise?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: This is only a resolution that we are discussing, and I would like the committee to agree to-night to let the resolution go through so that the Bill could be introduced. Then we can discuss it when it comes up again. Of course, if this were the last opportunity, I would certainly not think of the resolution going through tonight. There is a great difference of opinion in the House and I realize that very many of the members are sincere in their opposition to the resolution. It is a very important one. If the honourable member for Annapolis will agree to the resolutiongoing through so that the Bill can be printed, we can consider the matter again in committee and I will bring it up at an earlier time in the day so that we can have time to discuss it. The session is now nearing a close, and for that reason I am afraid that if we let the matter go over this evening and not have the Bill printed it will create much further delay. I would, therefore, appeal to hon. gentlemen to allow the resolution to pass.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
I have no desire at all to occupy unduly the attention of the House. As to private members sitting up till one o'clock in the morning, it is not a very serious matter to happen occasionally, but I do feel for the ministers who have grave problems to consider, and that in a serious spirit. It has been rumoured that there are fresh disturbances in Winnipeg to-day and I am sure the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, (Mr. Calder) who comes from the West, appreciates the gravity of the situation. For my part I should be anxious to permit the ministers

to retire and get some rest so that they could turn their attention early to-morrow to these matters. I do think, however, that before we can accede to the request of the Minister of Railways we should have an expression from him as to a serious purpose to print this Bill and to carry this legislation at the present session. Members are all anxious for the session to terminate within a reasonable period from the present. The printing of Bills costs money; but money does not seem to matter to a government like this. The matter of a $300,000,000 deficit does not seem to give a great deal of care to its supporters; I am afraid it will give a great deal of care to the country before we are very much older. We are continually getting fresh demands and you cannot pay a $300,000,000 deficit without money. Let me repeat, the printing of Bills costs money and I think before we undertake the printing of this Bill we should have a serious declaration either from the minister in charge or his chief henchman for this evening, the Minister of Colonization and Immigration, that there is a purpose to go on with this legislation this session and to carry the Bill through. If that be the serious purpose of the Government we from the West are not the men to use obstruction; we do not need to, we always think we advance arguments. The majority in this House must rule and if the majority want this money spent whether they know where it is going to come from or not, their view must prevail. But we should have an assertion from the minister that the Government intends to go on with this legislation and . carry it through this session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
There is another reason, which I have not yet advanced, why I think the committee should rise at this stage, if the .minister will pardon me. There are some members on this side who usually support the Government, who would be very unwilling to withhold their support from the Government on any occasion, and I flatter myself I am one of them. If the resolution is put through tonight with the present light that we have, even after listening to the luminous address of the hon. member from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), we are inclined to think we have not sufficient information to vote intelligently upon so vast and so in-1 a.m. volved a scheme. I think there are other members of this House

in the same position as myself in that regard. If we had time to consider this matter to think it out more definitely and study it more closely, and perhaps confer with the minister as to the details, we might be i na position where it would not be necessary to withhold our support. As it stands norw, I think I am speaking for others as well as myself when I say that is .the position. For that reason it would seem to me very desirable that the committee should be allowed to rise. This is the first time I have ever asked the indulgence of the Government in a matter of this kind, and it may very likely be the last. It will certainly give me a great deal of gratification if the minister oouild meet my wishes in this regard.

speechtext:
establish experimental farms in various parts of the country. In those farms scientific experiments are carried on, the results of which are beneficial to all parts of the Dominion, and in that way agriculture is helped. I want the same thing to be followed out in reference to roads. I think that the Federal Government might very properly engage in experimental road making. I am speaking in agreement with the views given me by the officer to whom I have just referred, when I say, that that department could use a much greater amount of money than it now has at its disposal. I believe the proper way for us to approach this question is for the Federal Government to build up a scientific department in road making, to gather together a body of engineers, and through their operations to be in a position, whenever a municipality or a province wants ' information in reference to this very important matter, to be able to give it to them, and to furnish them with competent and skilled help to make expenditures on road building.	,
But to-day there is not enough information and scientific knowledge on this question to warrant the expenditure of the exceedingly large sums of money which it is proposed to spend at this time of financial stringency. I venture to say, Mr. Chairman, that there is not one single province that has yet successfully grappled with the problem of road making. For years the various provinces have tinkered with this question. They have not gone at it in the right way. They decided that a certain road was needed and would cost a certain amount of money, and then they proceeded to get the money and to expend it without any previous experimental research, with the result that the expenditure in many cases has been lost. I do not think the province of Nova Scotia has suffered any more in this particular than the other provinces, but members of the present Government in Nova Scotia would be the first to admit that in the. past road construction has largely been a failure, and that to-day they are groping in the dark on this question, and if this Government forces the Government of Nova Scotia into the expenditure of large sums of money on road building, it will be spent in a hurry and practically thrown away.
I want to read to the House just a short paragraph from the Eastern Chronicle, a paper published in New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, in reference to some of the opera-

tions in connection with road building in that province. This is the paragraph:
There is one of two things wrong with the supposedly permanent culverts that have been placed along the highways of this country- either the design is had, or the work of installation was not properly done. That the costly work is more or less a failure is easily apparent to one travelling the roads. In places they have given way, have heen thrown up by the frost and are now a danger to travel rather than the maximum of safety they were originally designed to be. This will be a matter of deep regret to the county representatives who were responsible for the installation of these intended improvements, and who placed their faith in the engineer who prepared his plans, and the contractor who had the performance of the job. It looks very much as if the design of these culverts was really at fault.
The province of Nova Scotia borrowed a very large sum of money in good faith, and they yielded to the cry of immediate action in the construction of good roads. They put these culverts down without knowing how, without the proper staff to ensure the work being properly done. That is the long and short of it. The result is that that immense expenditure is worse than a total loss, because the roads in which those culverts were placed have been made dangerous.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to Nova Scotia generally, or just to certain counties?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext:
The paragraph I read had reference to a particular road in Nova Scotia, from my observation I may say that the condition described in the county of Pictou is characteristic of the various other parts of the province. The people of Nova Scotia want good roads; there is no doubt of that. It is needless to point out the merits of good roads; everybody realizes that they are necessary. But the question is, will the scheme that is now under consideration lead to the production of good roads in this country? In my judgment, it is doubtful whether it will. I believe-and I have the opinion of a very able expert to support my conclusion-that if this thing is carried through it will simply mean that huge sums of money will be passed on to the various provinces, which will thereupon engage in wild schemes of road-making and in two or three years there will be nothing whatever to show for all this expenditure. I agree with what the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) said the other evening when he spoke in favour of permanent roads. But it would be idle for us to borrow $20,-

000,000 and spend it in such a manner that in the future the only thing we shall have to remind us of the expenditure will be the necessity of our paying the indebtedness so incurred. 'Let us deal with this thing in a sane manner; let us continue the operations that have been started, go on with the work that has been begun, and wait until the provinces are in a better position to work intelligently upon the roads; then place the federal machinery at the disposal of the various provinces in order that they may build well. It is absolutely absurd for us to embark at this time upon such a scheme as this. I point out again the inadvisability of our trying to invade the jurisdiction of the provinces. The provinces do not want us to do so; we are trying as it were, to cast the mote out of their eye when there is the beam of heavy obligation in our own. In view of the heavy obligations under which we are staggering at the present time, it is very silly for us to go around the country looking for people whom we may help out.
This measure, Mr. Chairman, is one which requires all the united wisdom of the members of this House; I do not know of any measure that would require more careful scrutiny. It is an absolutely new departure; the Federal Government has never built roads in this country. No scientific investigation has been made by the Government; they are not in possession of any data on the subject; they are not able to give the House any information of a definite character, yet they are embarking upon a scheme involving the expenditure of millions of dollars. If this thing goes through,	every part	of	the country will be after the Federal Government to expend money on roads; we shall be in for a tremendous expenditure. This, therefore, is an inopportune time to try to force a measure of this kind through Parliament. The proper thing to do would have been to bring the Bill forward at an earlier period in the session and to refer it to- a special committee of the House for study, analysis and criticism. When we had to deal with the consolidation of the Railway Act a special committee was appointed and sat for diays considering the various clauses of that proposed Act. Railway problems were not new to us; yet we spent weeks in the committee giving very careful consideration to the details of this Railway Act. Now it is proposed, at the eleventh hour, a few days before prorogation, to embark upon an entirely new scheme, a scheme of which we are entirely ignorant; and it is proposed to rush it
through. An hon. gentleman asks the Government to allow the matter to stand until another day; that the vote be not taken at this time, but this request is refused by the minister, for reasons which no doubt he appreciates, but which I cannot for the life of me understand. There are many other things I wish to say on this subject; is the minister still obdurate?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext: I would be glad to do anything I could for the hon. member, but we have lost a good deal of time on this resolution, which is now before us for the third time. I make one more appeal to hon. gentlemen to let the resolution go through so that I may get the Bill printed. We will then have the second reading, when there will be opportunity for discussion; and it may be further discussed in committee. Of course, if the hon. mensjber wishes to finish his remarks, I will give consideration to his suggestions. I realize that this is one of the most important measures that ever came before this House, but it -has passed this Parliament twice before, and it is well known to hon. members and to the people. The member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) wants to know whether we are going on with this Bill. I am asking that it be passed; then we may consider whether it, with other Bills, shall be gone on with during the present session. But I am not going to drop it in this way. T am as anxious as any member of the House is that the session be brought to a close at the earliest possible day, and if we do not get this resolution through to-night it will be the first Order of the Day to-morrow. If we pass the resolution to-night, we shall save a day and members will get home that much earlier. That is the reason why I ask that the resolution go through. There are a lot of other Bills on the Order Paper. In previous sessions Bills have been dropped in order that the session might be brought to a close. I am willing to do anything to facilitate the work of the session, but if the resolution is not adopted to-night I will ask the House to take it up to-morrow and to discuss it tomorrow and from day to day to see if we cannot have the resolution passed so that the Bill may be introduced.

That Bill was entirely different from this oift and involved an entirely different principle. It is one of the principles of responsible government that the Government which collects the taxes shall be responsible for the expenditure of the money so collected. That was the principle involved in the Highways Bills, which was passed by this House and killed in the Senate.
That is not the principle embodied in this legislation. I do not want to be churlish in this matter. My only reason for opposing this resolution is in order that all the members of this House may appreciate its importance and significance. If the minister would consent to have this Bill sent to a special committee to be considered carefully, as I believe it should be considered, I would have no objection to the resolution being allowed to pass.

speechtext: I will bring the matter before Council, and we will decide whether it will be better to refer the Bill to a special committee at this late stage of the session or submit it to the House. That is a matter I should not like to decide offhand myself, but I shall certainly bring the matter before the Government and let my hon. friend know. I really think it would save time and shorten the session if this resolution were allowed to pass and we could get the Bill printed and on the Order Paper, and a copy of it in the hands of every member.

I regret if I appear to have wasted the time of the House unnecessarily. I addressed what I thought was a courteous request to my hon. friend, and if it embarrassed him, I am sorry indeed; I did not mean it that way. I regret also that the minister should have used something which appeared very, very like a threat, and addressed particularly to myself. He assured me in somewhat strong language that if this resolution does not pass to-night it will be the first thing tomorrow. That will not incommode me. This House has been four months in session and I have not missed a Parliamentary day, and if my hon. friend wants me to stay here with him four months longer, and his constitution holds out, I will stay with him. I would remind him that on one occasion when we were sitting opposite to one another we had a two weeks' sitting without any intermission whatever. I regret that he should have thrown out what appeared to be very, very like a threat. I repeat what I said before, that if it should be the wish of the majority to enact this legis-

lation I have no objection; it would not be any use if I had. I desire majorities to rule. I have expressed the wish that we had been given a clear explanation of what it is the Government wants to do in the way of road building.
This has not been an idle day in Parliament. We had a very long Bill brought in by the (Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) this morning, a lucid exposition of the Bill greatly facilitated its passage, and it went through all its sixty-four clauses in committee. We had also a Bill with a great many clauses in connection with technical education. I must say, if the minister is inclined to threaten, that we would have got further ahead if he had told us exactly where he stands in regard to this national highway proposition and the other proposals. If he had told us exactly what the legislation is meant to effect, he would have helped me sooner to have ceased talking, and would have helped to let the resolution pass so far as I was concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext: The last thing in the world I would wish to use is a threat, and if my remarks could be construed in any way as a threat, I would certainly wish to withdraw them and apologize to the House. I realize that there is a great opposition to this legislation in the House. This is the third time I have tried to get this resolution through.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext: What I felt about it was this: If I am not to get the resolution through to-night, I would rather take it up first thing to-morrow and let the whole House decide whether we were to go on with it. I did not feel that I was asking anything unreasonable to let the resolution pass so that the Bill could be printed. I did not wish to threaten in any way, but I wished to get this Bill printed. We have a lot of other Bills on the Order Paper, and as far as I am concerned I will do everything I can to try and bring the session to a close, even if it should be necessary to drop this or some other Bills; but the Government must decide whether it shall be proceeded with or not.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
I considered the intimation of the minister that if this resolution did not pass to-night it would be the first order of business to-morrow, not as a threat,

but as a promise which was due to certain members of this House who do not agree with the position of the hon. member for Red Deer and the hon. member for Annapolis, but desire this resolution to go through. While I am on my feet I should like to make one observation regarding the argument advanced by the hon. member for Annapolis with respect to the British North America Act and the infringement on provincial rights. Before this resolution came up he gave his consent to the passing of the Bill respecting technical education, and if there is any argument in regard to the invasion of provincial rights that can be used against this resolution it can be applied with equal force to the Bill on technical education involving an expenditure of $10,000,000, to which the hon. member has given his consent.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext: In order to set myself straight, let me say that I have no inconsistency in this matter. I was opposed to the principle of the Bill on technical education, and if a vote had been taken on it I would have been compelled to vote against it for exactly the same reason that I am opposed to this resolution.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: AID TO PROVINCES FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
speechtext:
If it is the will of the minister that a vote should be taken on this resolution to-night I shall have to take up a little of the time of the Committee, because I have not said a word on the principle involved. I have said that this is an inopportune time for the legislation to come before the House. This legislation is entirely wrong in principle It is an infringement of the rights of the provinces, and unless they have changed their minds I do not think they are a unit in accepting it. The last Highway Bill was killed for almost exactly the same reason. If we are going to hold a string on this grant-and we are holding a string on it-I can tell the minister that Saskatchewan, at all events, is absolutely opposed to the Dominion Government handing over moneys with a string attached. If the minister insists on a vote to-night, I shall have to take up a little time. As the minister does not care to answer, I take it for granted that he intends that a vote shall be taken to-night. In the first place, the emphatic statement of the minister that the Dominion Government would hold a string on the grant is surely sufficient reason for any member of this House opposing it. The minister says to the provinces: "We are prepared to give you this money, but we are going to say just exactly where you are going to build this road and the kind of
material you shall use in building it. We are going to keep an absolute string on the grant." For that is what the minister's statement meant. It is all very well to say that it will be a matter of agreement, but that does not work. The Dominion Government will hold a string on this money continuously. I say the principle is absolutely wrong.
The Technical Education Bill has no such string on it. It says the money must be spent for technical education but does not stipulate that one or two colleges must be built or that this or the other subject must be taught. It is simply provided for technical education. But this Bill says you must build the road where this Government will be satisfied with it, and the Government must be satisfied with the construction and the material. It has an absolutely binding string on it from start to finish.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext: The matter of cost is in the opinion of the minister, too.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext:
I did not know that, but that makes it so much worse. It seems to me most unreasonable to ask the provincial governments to accept this regulation, and I do not think that many of them will do so. Let the minister give us the information he has secured from the governments as to what they will do. If he is prepared to tell me that the government of my province will allow the Dominion Government to have complete control in the matter I shall immediately withdraw my objection, for that is the provincial government's business, and his assurance to that effect will relieve me of responsibility. But in the absence of that, and speaking, as I think I am, for the people of my province, I am opposed to the methods proposed. This was the attitude of the people of my province some years ago and I do not think they have altered their opinions much in this respect. We believe in provincial autonomy and although we were not accorded the-fullest measure of it, still we got a fair degree of autonomy and are anxious to retain it and if possible have it extended. To permit the Dominion Government to interfere with the internal affairs of a province is entirely wrong. We have heard a good deal about the United States methods. I am not familiar with many states, but I am fairly well acquainted with the good roads scheme in Michigan, as I have a brother there who is connected with municipal works. There the state hands the money to the county and an

arrangement is entered into between tbem. The county lays down the plan of the road and the Federal Government has nothing whatever to do with the work. If this Government is prepared to hand the money to the provinces and let them and the municipalities work out their own salvation I will withdraw 'my objection now and when the Bill comes before the Committee. Otherwise, I shall have to oppose it in Committee as strenuously as possible. I am not opposed to good roads, but I want the Provincial Government and the people of the province to say where those roads shall be built. In our own province they get away as far as they can from roads as such. They only undertake now large contracts, such as heavy fills or bridges. A member of the Government was Minister of Highways there for several years, and he will tell you they have been getting away from that system as much as possible. It was a continual source of trouble, getting the minister into difficulties through no fault of his own. This is a re-introduction of the system in an intensified form. It is entirely unwarranted and should not be supported. There are other matters I would like to touch upon and I should like to say a word or two to our British Columbia friends, but as the hour is late I will refrain from further remarks.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Hon. Mr. REID thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 152 founded on the resolution.
Motion agreed to -and Bill read the first time.
